e: From Middle English axen, aksen, axien, from Old English ācsian and āxian, showing metathesis from āscian. Ax/aks was common in literary works until about 1600.
q: When they were come togedder, they axed off hym, sayinge: Master wilt thou at this tyme restore agayne the kyngdom of israhel?
1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts:
Dolly: And if so be, why did you ax me to keep you company? Housekeeper wants me below to pick raisins.
1836, Joanna Baillie, The Alienated Manor, act 4:
"Thin the masther called out Dinny Moran, an' dhragged him up to one o' the Dublin young ladies, an' bid Dinny be stout an' ax her out to dance wid him."
1850, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, London: H.G. Bohn, page 517:

Ar try who'l ax em the hardest riddle,
Ar soonest vind out oone put us, true...
